rv.q: In this poetic, heightened comedy of mourning and oblivion, the surest, most steadying love is between parent and grown child.
With Waters’s hand guiding you, it’s worth pressing your ear to the poetry of Ruhl’s work all over again.
That wordless sequence is the play’s most transfixing moment.
Scenic designer Scott Bradley’s set, along with James’s and Hawke’s performances, make this somewhat uneven revival worth the trek through the rain — just don’t forget your underworld umbrella.
But “Eurydice” could use a lot more splendor, and a lot more song.
For me, Eurydice is a play that one wants to like more than one does.

cn.t: Ruhl's inventive reimagining of the Greek myth earns praise for its imaginative staging and design, though critics are divided on the play's emotional impact and quirky approach to the classic story.
